paras: The killing of Oscar Carmichael was the shooting of an escaped Georgia convict by a posse at his wife's house in or near Henry County, Georgia, on the night of Friday, November 16, 1888, hours after he was accused of killing his guard, W. J. Gresham, near Griffin. Reports said the posse "riddled" him with shot or bullets, and differed on whether he died in an exchange of fire or was fired on as he approached the house. A Griffin wire story about the guard's death and the bloodhound chase ran in papers from Minnesota to Texas under headlines such as "Speedy Vengeance Overtakes a Prisoner Who Murdered His Guard."

According to the Savannah Morning News, T. G. Manly Jr. worked a few convicts on his plantation about four miles from Griffin, and on the morning of November 16 he had seven of them clearing new ground under a guard named W. J. Gresham. The wire version placed the men in "the camp near Sunnyside" and said four convicts were on a detail under Guard Gresham. None of the reports states the race of Carmichael or of Gresham.

The Morning News's Griffin correspondent, writing the same day, said Carmichael was cutting down a tree when Gresham passed within reach, and that he struck the guard over the right eye with his axe and then struck him three more times. Carmichael then took Gresham's pistol and gun, marched the other convicts about a mile ahead of him, and turned them back at gunpoint, and they returned to give the alarm. The wire story instead had Carmichael kill the guard with a thrown stone, after which all four prisoners escaped. A large posse set out, and by 2 o'clock it had found where he had stopped to try to remove his shackles; the correspondent closed with the line "He will be lynched if caught."

The wire account said the sheriff, with a posse and two bloodhounds, followed the trail through swamps into Henry County and learned that the fugitive had gone to the house where his wife lived. On Friday night, by this account, the posse surrounded the house and fire was opened, and after several volleys Carmichael rushed out brandishing a revolver and was "riddled with shot from the Sheriff's officers."

The Morning News gave another version on November 20, saying Carmichael "is reported" to have been killed that Friday night at his wife's house near the Henry line. In that account the sheriff had gone back to town, while the posse went to the house, watched for him, and fired on him when he was seen approaching.
No report of an inquest or other inquiry into the shooting appears in the coverage.

The Griffin dispatch, dated November 19, appeared that day in the San Antonio Daily Light, the Waterbury Evening Democrat and a Delaware Evening Journal, and on November 20 in the Wheeling Daily Intelligencer, the Memphis Appeal and the St. Paul Daily Globe. Weeklies in Kansas and Indian Territory reprinted it on November 22, the Indian Chieftain naming the dead guard "Guard Carmichael," while the Waterbury and Delaware printings called the convict "Arthur Carmichael." A one-sentence digest of the story ran in Tennessee and Kentucky papers on November 21 and 23, and a Chicago weekly's digest on November 24 dated the shooting "on Monday."

Headlines treated the posse's shooting as punishment: "Speedy Vengeance Overtakes a Prisoner Who Murdered His Guard," "A Southern Sheriff Gets the Best of a Convict Murderer," and "A Convict Run Down and Killed by a Sheriff's Posse." The dispatch called him "the fugitive murderer" and did not question the killing. The Savannah Morning News carried details the wire lacked, including the axe and the prediction of a lynching, and hedged the posse's killing as what was "reported."

The local and wire accounts disagree on the weapon (an axe or a stone) and on whether the other convicts escaped or were turned back. On the shooting, the wire has the sheriff's officers firing during an exchange of volleys, while the Morning News has the posse, without the sheriff, firing on him as he approached. Only the Chicago digest dates the shooting to Monday rather than Friday night.

reader.title: Killing of Oscar Carmichael
bases: A sheriff's posse tracked the escaped convict with bloodhounds and shot him at his wife's house (A5, A8).

A posse shot dead a convict accused of killing his guard (A5, A8), and the local paper predicted a lynching (A1); but the wire says he was armed and exchanging fire with the sheriff's officers (A5), while the Morning News says the sheriff had left and the posse fired on sight (A8), so whether the killing was without lawful authority is unclear.
The Savannah Morning News's Georgia paragraphs (A8) and the separate Griffin wire story (A5) both report the posse killing Carmichael at his wife's house, though they differ on details.

accounts.label: Savannah Morning News Griffin correspondent (Nov. 16)
accounts.gist: Carmichael killed Gresham with an axe, took his pistol and gun, turned the other convicts back, and fled; a large posse pursued and 'He will be lynched if caught.'

accounts.label: Griffin wire report (Nov. 19)
accounts.gist: Carmichael killed the guard with a stone; the sheriff's posse tracked him with bloodhounds to his wife's house, exchanged volleys, and riddled him as he rushed out with a revolver.

accounts.label: Savannah Morning News Georgia paragraphs (Nov. 20)
accounts.gist: The sheriff returned to town; the posse watched the wife's house and fired on Carmichael as he approached, reportedly riddling him with bullets.

accounts.label: Chicago weekly digest
accounts.gist: Carmichael was surrounded at his wife's house on Monday and riddled with bullets.

framing.detail: Wire headlines: 'Speedy Vengeance Overtakes a Prisoner Who Murdered His Guard', 'A Southern Sheriff Gets the Best of a Convict Murderer'; text calls him 'the fugitive murderer'.
Savannah Morning News headed the guard's killing 'Cold-Blooded Murder', predicted a lynching, and reported the posse killing as hearsay ('according to reports').
Digest papers condensed the wire into one sentence ending 'The pursuing posse riddled him with bullets.'

conflicts.note: The same-day local Griffin correspondence (A1) is closer to the event than the wire.

versions.value: seven convicts; Carmichael marched them a mile and turned them back, and they gave the alarm
house surrounded, volleys exchanged, Carmichael rushed out with a revolver and was shot by the sheriff's officers
sheriff gone back to town; posse watched the house and fired on him as he approached

conflicts.note: Both are second-hand; the Morning News marks its version as reports.
The Monday date appears only in a later Chicago digest; Friday night is in both fuller reports.
